summary: A 1977 description of the SUPDUP protocol, a remote terminal protocol developed at MIT that supports display terminals better than plain Telnet. It is historic.

eli5.summary: A remote screen that handled cursors and fancy displays better than other tools did. This explains how it worked.

subtitle: A display-oriented remote terminal protocol

tldr.problem: Plain Telnet and other remote login protocols could not take advantage of display terminals' capabilities like cursor positioning, erase functions, and insert/delete operations.
tldr.mechanism: SUPDUP is a remote terminal protocol developed at MIT that defines a virtual display terminal using a set of display operations and codes common to all terminals. It supports cursor motion, selective erase, character and line insert/delete, and handles both simple TTY terminals and advanced display terminals.
tldr.outcome: SUPDUP was widely used at MIT and a few other sites for remote access to ITS systems, providing a much richer display experience than Telnet. It is now historic, replaced by modern remote access technologies.

today: RFC 734 is Historic. SUPDUP was specific to MIT ITS systems and never achieved widespread adoption. Modern remote access uses SSH with terminal emulators that provide far richer capabilities.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The SUPDUP protocol originated as the internal protocol used by ITS (Incompatible Timesharing System) for terminal control at MIT. Unlike Telnet, which works with any terminal type, SUPDUP defines a virtual display terminal with a set of operations common to all display terminals: cursor positioning, character and line insertion/deletion, selective screen erase, and bell.

The protocol is device-independent and can run on terminals ranging from simple printing Teletypes to advanced display terminals with full cursor control. SUPDUP also supports terminals missing any set of features, gracefully degrading to match capabilities.
sections.eli5: SUPDUP is like a language for talking to smart terminal screens. It says 'move the cursor here' or 'erase this line' without caring what brand of screen you have. Dumb screens that cannot do fancy things just skip those commands.

sections.title: Initialization and Operations
sections.content:
The SUPDUP server listens on socket 137 (octal). After connection, the user sends terminal capabilities to the server using 36-bit words sent as six 6-bit bytes. The capabilities include screen height (TCMXV), screen width (TCMXH), scrolling glitch count (TTYROL), and feature bits indicating support for cursor movement, erase operations, overprinting, insert/delete, and other features.

Server output uses %TD codes (display codes) to control the terminal: %TDMOV moves the cursor to a position, %TDEOL erases to end of line, %TDCRL clears a line, %TDILP and %TDDLP insert and delete lines, %TDICP and %TDDCP insert and delete characters. Codes less than 200 (octal) are ordinary printing characters.
sections.eli5: When you connect, you tell SUPDUP what your screen can do (how big, can it move the cursor, can it erase). Then the computer sends special codes to move your cursor, clear lines, and insert or delete. If your screen cannot do something, it just ignores that code.

sections.title: Character Input and Special Modes
sections.content:
SUPDUP supports two character sets: 7-bit ASCII and 12-bit extended ASCII with bucky bits (modifier keys) for CONTROL, META, and TOP. Input characters with bucky bits are escaped using a special protocol: 034 (octal) followed by a byte with the bucky bits shifted, then the character. This allows terminals to send modified keystrokes like <CONTROL><META>[LINE FEED].

The protocol supports output reset (aborting output in progress on network interrupt), operation on terminals as simple as a Teletype model 33, and has reserved space for future extensions. The server may process output reset requests and handle terminal-specific character mappings for the extended Stanford/ITS character set.
sections.eli5: Your keyboard might send not just 'a' but a modified key like control-a or meta-a. SUPDUP has a special way to send those to the computer. The whole thing is designed to work with any kind of screen, even ancient ones.
